abstractedness: The state of being abstracted; abstract character.
abscess: A collection of pus or purulent matter in any tissue or organ of the body, the result of a morbid process. ableminded: Having much intellectual power. -- A`ble-mind"ed*ness, n.
abusive: 1. Wrongly used; perverted; misapplied. I am . . . necessitated to use the word Parliament improperly, according to the abusive acceptation thereof. Fuller. 2. Given to misusing; also, full of abuses. (old) "The abusive prerogatives of his see." Hallam. 3. Practicing abuse; prone to ill treat by coarse, insulting words or by other ill usage; as, an abusive author;
ablegation: The act of sending abroad. (old) Jer. Taylor.
abaxial: Away from the axis or central line; eccentric. Balfour.
abbatial: Belonging to an abbey; as, abbatial rights.
abalone: A univalve mollusk of the genus Haliotis. The shell is lined with mother-of-pearl, and used for ornamental purposes; the sea-ear. Several large species are found on the coast of California, clinging closely to the rocks.
abbotship: The state or office of an abbot.
abhorrence: Extreme hatred or detestation; the feeling of utter dislike.
abash: To destroy the self-possession of; to confuse or confound, as by exciting suddenly a consciousness of guilt, mistake, or inferiority; to put to shame; to disconcert; to discomfit. Abashed, the devil stood, And felt how awful goodness is. Milton. He was a man whom no check could abash. Macaulay. Syn. -- To confuse; confound; disconcert; shame. -- To Abash, Confuse, Confound.
abelian: One of a sect in Africa (4th century), mentioned by St. Augustine, who states that they married, but lived in continence, after the manner, as they pretended, of Abel.
absinthate: A combination of absinthic acid with a base or positive radical.
abolishment: The act of abolishing; abolition; destruction. Hooker.
abecedary: Pertaining to, or formed by, the letters of the alphabet; alphabetic; hence, rudimentary. Abecedarian psalms, hymns, etc., compositions in which (like the 119th psalm in Hebrew) distinct portions or… | A primer; the first principle or rudiment of anything. Fuller.
abscession: A separating; removal; also, an abscess. (old) Gauden. Barrough.
absterge: To make clean by wiping; to wipe away; to cleanse; hence, to purge. Quincy.
absent: 1. Being away from a place; withdrawn from a place; not present. "Expecting absent friends." Shak. 2. Not existing; lacking; as, the part was rudimental or absent. 3. abelite: One of a sect in Africa (4th century), mentioned by St. Augustine, who states that they married, but lived in continence, after the manner, as they pretended, of Abel.
abrenounce: To renounce. (old) "They abrenounce and cast them off." Latimer.
abaft: Behind; toward the stern from; as, abaft the wheelhouse. Abaft the beam. See under Beam. | Toward the stern; aft; as, to go abaft.
aboriginal: 1. First; original; indigenous; primitive; native; as, the aboriginal tribes of America. "Mantled o'er with aboriginal turf." Wordsworth. 2. Of or pertaining to aborigines; | 1. An original inhabitant of any land; one of the aborigines. 2. An animal or a plant native to the region. It may well be doubted whether this frog is an aboriginal of these islands. Darwin.
abortionist: One who procures abortion or miscarriage.
abdicate: 1. To surrender or relinquish, as sovereign power; to withdraw definitely from filling or exercising, as a high office, station, dignity; as, to abdicate the throne, the crown, the papacy. | To relinquish or renounce a throne, or other high office or dignity. Though a king may abdicate for his own person, he cannot abdicate for the monarchy. Burke.
abbreviatory: Serving or tending to abbreviate; shortening; abridging.
ab: The fifth month of the Jewish year according to the ecclesiastical reckoning, the eleventh by the civil computation, coinciding nearly with August. W. Smith.
abolitionism: The principles or measures of abolitionists. Wilberforce.
abstersive: Something cleansing. The strong abstersive of some heroic magistrate. Milton.
ably: A suffix composed of -able and the adverbial suffix -ly; as, favorably.
abnegator: One who abnegates, denies, or rejects anything.
abiogenesis: The supposed origination of living organisms from lifeless matter; such genesis as does not involve the action of living parents; spontaneous generation; -- called also abiogeny, and opposed to biogenesis. abalienation: The act of abalienating; alienation; estrangement. (old)
abraxas: A mystical word used as a charm and engraved on gems among the ancients; also, a gem stone thus engraved.
abluvion: That which is washed off. Dwight.
abirritate: To diminish the sensibility of; to debilitate.
abnet: The girdle of a Jewish priest or officer.
abstemiousness: The quality of being abstemious, temperate, or sparing in the use of food and strong drinks. It expresses a greater degree of abstinence than temperance.
abjunctive: Exceptional. It is this power which leads on from the accidental and abjunctive to the universal. I. Taylor.
abidance: The state of abiding; abode; continuance; compliance (with). The Christians had no longer abidance in the holy hill of Palestine. Fuller. A judicious abidance by rules. Helps.
ablebodied: Having a sound, strong body; physically competent; robust. "Able-bodied vagrant." Froude. -- A`ble-bod"ied*ness, n..
abator: (a) One who abates a nuisance. (b) A person who, without right, enters into a freehold on the death of the last possessor, before the heir or devisee. Blackstone.
abasia: Inability to coördinate muscular actions properly in walking. - - A*ba"sic (#), a.
abord: Manner of approaching or accosting; address. Chesterfield. | To approach; to accost. (old) Digby.
abatement: 1. The act of abating, or the state of being abated; a lessening, diminution, or reduction; removal or putting an end to; as, the abatement of a nuisance is the suppression thereof. 2. The amount abated; that which is taken away by way of reduction; deduction; decrease; a rebate or discount allowed. 3. (Her.) A mark of dishonor on an escutcheon. 4.
abstractitious: Obtained from plants by distillation. (old) Crabb.
abjectness: The state of being abject; abasement; meanness; servility. Grew.
abider: 1. One who abides, or continues. (old) "Speedy goers and strong abiders." Sidney. 2. One who dwells; a resident. Speed.
abdest: Purification by washing the hands before prayer; -- a Mohammedan rite. Heyse.
abduce: To draw or conduct away; to withdraw; to draw to a different part. (old) If we abduce the eye unto either corner, the object will not duplicate. Sir T. Browne.
abranchiata: A group of annelids, so called because the species composing it have no special organs of respiration.
abecedarian: 1. One who is learning the alphabet; hence, a tyro. 2. One engaged in teaching the alphabet. Wood. | Pertaining to, or formed by, the letters of the alphabet; alphabetic; hence, rudimentary. Abecedarian psalms, hymns, etc., compositions in which (like the 119th psalm in Hebrew) distinct portions or…
ablaze: 1. On fire; in a blaze, gleaming. Milman. All ablaze with crimson and gold. Longfellow. 2. In a state of glowing excitement or ardent desire. The young Cambridge democrats were all ablaze to assist Torrijos. Carlyle.
abrahamman: One of a set of vagabonds who formerly roamed through England, feigning lunacy for the sake of obtaining alms. Nares. To sham Abraham, to feign sickness. Goldsmith.
abatvoix: The sounding-board over a pulpit or rostrum.
abundance: An overflowing fullness; ample sufficiency; great plenty; profusion; copious supply; superfluity; wealth: -- strictly applicable to quantity only, but sometimes used of number. It is lamentable to remember what abundance of noble blood hath been shed with small benefit to the Christian state. Raleigh. Syn. -- Exuberance; plenteousness; plenty; copiousness; overflow; riches;
abdominales: A group including the greater part of fresh-water fishes, and many marine ones, having the ventral fins under the abdomen behind the pectorals.
absinth: 1. The plant absinthium or common wormwood. 2. A strong spirituous liqueur made from wormwood and brandy or alcohol.
abdominous: Having a protuberant belly; pot-bellied. Gorgonius sits, abdominous and wan, Like a fat squab upon a Chinese fan. Cowper.
abietene: A volatile oil distilled from the resin or balsam of the nut pine (Pinus sabiniana) of California.
aberrant: See Aberr.] 1. Wandering; straying from the right way. 2. (Biol.) Deviating from the ordinary or natural type; exceptional; abnormal. The more aberrant any form is, the greater must have been the number of connecting forms which, on my theory, have been exterminated. Darwin.
absorptiveness: The quality of being absorptive; absorptive power.
abnegation: a denial; a renunciation. With abnegation of God, of his honor, and of religion, they may retain the friendship of the court. Knox.
abstractedly: In an abstracted manner; separately; with absence of mind.
abortion: 1. The act of giving premature birth; particularly, the expulsion of the human fetus prematurely, or before it is capable of sustaining life; miscarriage. abelonian: One of a sect in Africa (4th century), mentioned by St. Augustine, who states that they married, but lived in continence, after the manner, as they pretended, of Abel.
abies: A genus of coniferous trees, properly called Fir, as the balsam fir and the silver fir. The spruces are sometimes also referred to this genus.
aboriginality: The quality of being aboriginal. Westm. Rev.
absence: 1. A state of being absent or withdrawn from a place or from companionship; -- opposed to presence. Not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence. Phil. ii. 12. 2. abased: 1. Lowered; humbled. 2. (Her.) Etym: [F. abaissé.] Borne lower than usual, as a fess; also, having the ends of the wings turned downward towards the point of the shield.
abietic: Of or pertaining to the fir tree or its products; as, abietic acid, called also sylvic acid. Watts.
abc: 1. The first three letters of the alphabet, used for the whole alphabet. 2. A primer for teaching the alphabet and first elements of reading. (old) 3. The simplest rudiments of any subject; as, the A B C of finance. A B C book, a primer. Shak.
absorbing: Swallowing, engrossing; as, an absorbing pursuit. -- Ab*sorb"ing, adv.
abderian: Given to laughter; inclined to foolish or incessant merriment.
abuse: 1. To put to a wrong use; to misapply; to misuse; to put to a bad use; to use for a wrong purpose or end; to pervert; as, to abuse inherited gold; to make an excessive use of; | 1. Improper treatment or use; application to a wrong or bad purpose; misuse; as, an abuse of our natural powers; an abuse of civil rights, or of privileges or advantages; an abuse of language.
able: An adjective suffix now usually in a passive sense; able to be; fit to be; expressing capacity or worthiness in a passive sense; as, movable, able to be moved; amendable, able to be amended; blamable, fit to be blamed; salable. abscind: To cut off. "Two syllables . . . abscinded from the rest." Johnson.
abatable: Capable of being abated; as, an abatable writ or nuisance.
abrahamic: Pertaining to Abraham, the patriarch; as, the Abrachamic covenant.
abaca: The Manila-hemp plant (Musa textilis); also, its fiber. See Manila hemp under Manila.
abstention: The act of abstaining; a holding aloof. Jer. Taylor.

abominably: In an abominable manner; very odiously; detestably.
abuttal: The butting or boundary of land, particularly at the end; a headland. Spelman.

aberr: To wander; to stray. (old) Sir T. Browne.
aboma: A large South American serpent (Boa aboma).
abandonment: 1. The act of abandoning, or the state of being abandoned; total desertion; relinquishment. The abandonment of the independence of Europe. Burke. 2. (Mar. abide: 1. To wait; to pause; to delay. (old) Chaucer. 2. abuser: One who abuses [in the various senses of the verb].
absonous: Discordant; inharmonious; incongruous. (old) "Absonous to our reason." Glanvill.

absentation: The act of absenting one's self. Sir W. Hamilton.
abusiveness: The quality of being abusive; rudeness of language, or violence to the person. Pick out mirth, like stones out of thy ground, Profaneness, filthiness, abusiveness. Herbert.
abasement: The act of abasing, humbling, or bringing low; the state of being abased or humbled; humiliation.
ability: The quality or state of being able; power to perform, whether physical, moral, intellectual, conventional, or legal; capacity; skill or competence in doing; sufficiency of strength, skill, resources, etc.; -- in the plural, faculty, talent. abrenunciation: Absolute renunciation or repudiation. (old) An abrenunciation of that truth which he so long had professed, and still believed. Fuller.
abetment: The act of abetting; as, an abetment of treason, crime, etc.
abnodation: The act of cutting away the knots of trees. Crabb.
abyss: 1. A bottomless or unfathomed depth, gulf, or chasm; hence, any deep, immeasurable, and, specifically, hell, or the bottomless pit. Ye powers and spirits of this nethermost abyss. Milton. abjection: 1. The act of bringing down or humbling. "The abjection of the king and his realm." Joe. 2. The state of being rejected or cast out. ablen: A small fresh-water fish (Leuciscus alburnus); the bleak.
abrogative: Tending or designed to abrogate; as, an abrogative law.
abutilon: A genus of malvaceous plants of many species, found in the torrid and temperate zones of both continents; -- called also Indian mallow.
aboutsledge: The largest hammer used by smiths. Weale.
abstractiveness: The quality of being abstractive; abstractive property.
abseybook: An A-B-C book; a primer. (old) Shak.

abditory: A place for hiding or preserving articles of value. Cowell.
abraumsalts: A red ocher used to darken mahogany and for making chloride of potassium.

abnormous: Abnormal; irregular. Hallam. A character of a more abnormous cast than his equally suspected coadjutor. State Trials.

abderite: An inhabitant of Abdera, in Thrace. The Abderite, Democritus, the Laughing Philosopher.

abreuvoir: The joint or interstice between stones, to be filled with mortar. Gwilt.
abstractly: In an abstract state or manner; separately; absolutely; by itself; as, matter abstractly considered.
abstinent: Refraining from indulgence, especially from the indulgence of appetite; abstemious; continent; temperate. Beau. & Fl. | 1. One who abstains. 2. (Eccl. Hist.) One of a sect who appeared in France and Spain in the 3d century.
aberrancy: State of being aberrant; a wandering from the right way; deviation from truth, rectitude, etc. Aberrancy of curvature (Geom.), the deviation of a curve from a circular form.
abodement: A foreboding; an omen. (old) "Abodements must not now affright us." Shak.
abdominalia: A group of cirripeds having abdominal appendages.
ablactation: 1. The weaning of a child from the breast, or of young beasts from their dam. Blount. 2. (Hort.) The process of grafting now called inarching, or grafting by approach.
abaction: Stealing cattle on a large scale. (old)
abdication: The act of abdicating; the renunciation of a high office, dignity, or trust, by its holder; commonly the voluntary renunciation of sovereign power; as, abdication of the throne, government, power, authority.
above: 1. In or to a higher place; higher than; on or over the upper surface; over; -- opposed to below or beneath. Fowl that may fly above the earth. Gen. i. 20. 2. Figuratively, higher than; | 1. abstractive: Having the power of abstracting; of an abstracting nature. "The abstractive faculty." I. Taylor.
abaser: He who, or that which, abases.
abramman: One of a set of vagabonds who formerly roamed through England, feigning lunacy for the sake of obtaining alms. Nares. To sham Abraham, to feign sickness. Goldsmith.
abstemious: 1. Abstaining from wine. [Orig. Latin sense.] Under his special eye Abstemious I grew up and thrived amain. Milton. 2. abater: One who, or that which, abates.

abnormal: Not conformed to rule or system; deviating from the type; anomalous; irregular. "That deviating from the type; anomalous; irregular. " Froude.
abanga: A West Indian palm; also the fruit of this palm, the seeds of which are used as a remedy for diseases of the chest.
abiogenist: One who believes that life can be produced independently of antecedent. Huxley.
abirritation: A pathological condition opposite to that of irritation; debility; want of strength; asthenia.
abrasion: 1. The act of abrading, wearing, or rubbing off; the wearing away by friction; as, the abrasion of coins. 2. The substance rubbed off. Berkeley. 3. (Med.) A superficial excoriation, with loss of substance under the form of small shreds. Dunglison.
abassi: A silver coin of Persia, worth about twenty cents.
abattoir: A public slaughterhouse for cattle, sheep, etc.
abdominoscopy: Examination of the abdomen to detect abdominal disease.

absentee: One who absents himself from his country, office, post, or duty; especially, a landholder who lives in another country or district than that where his estate is situated; as, an Irish absentee. Macaulay.

ablude: To be unlike; to differ. (old) Bp. Hall.
abhorrent: 1. Abhorring; detesting; having or showing abhorrence; loathing; hence, strongly opposed to; as, abhorrent thoughts. The persons most abhorrent from blood and treason. Burke. abaciscus: One of the tiles or squares of a tessellated pavement; an abaculus.
abele: The white polar (Populus alba). Six abeles i' the churchyard grow. Mrs. Browning.

absolutely: In an absolute, independent, or unconditional manner; wholly; positively.
abstersiveness: The quality of being abstersive. Fuller.

abacinate: To blind by a red-hot metal plate held before the eyes.

abler: comp. of Able. -- A"blest, a., superl. of Able.

abbacy: The dignity, estate, or jurisdiction of an abbot.
ableness: Ability of body or mind; force; vigor. [Obs. or R.]
abstractness: The quality of being abstract. "The abstractness of the ideas." Locke.
abacus: 1. A table or tray strewn with sand, anciently used for drawing, calculating, etc. (old) 2. ablins: Perhaps; possibly. [Scotch] Burns. AICH'S METAL Aich's met"al. A kind of gun metal, containing copper, zinc, and iron, but no tin.
abatis: A means of defense formed by felled trees, the ends of whose branches are sharpened and directed outwards, or against the enemy.
aback: 1. Toward the back or rear; backward. "Therewith aback she started." Chaucer. 2. Behind; in the rear. Knolles. 3. (Naut.) Backward against the mast;-said of the sails when pressed by the wind. abscond: 1. To hide, withdraw, or be concealed. The marmot absconds all winter. Ray. 2. To depart clandestinely; to steal off and secrete one's self; -- used especially of persons who withdraw to avoid a… | To hide; to conceal. (old) Bentley.
abrood: In the act of brooding. (old) Abp. Sancroft.

abstergent: Serving to cleanse, detergent. | A substance used in cleansing; a detergent; as, soap is an abstergent.

abacist: One who uses an abacus in casting accounts; a calculator.
abominableness: The quality or state of being abominable; odiousness. Bentley.
absinthial: Of or pertaining to wormwood; absinthian.
abeam: On the beam, that is, on a line which forms a right angle with the ship's keel; opposite to the center of the ship's side.
ablaqueate: To lay bare, as the roots of a tree. (old) Bailey.
abraid: To awake; to arouse; to stir or start up; also, to shout out. (old) Chaucer.
absinthin: The bitter principle of wormwood (Artemisia absinthium). Watts.
abolitionist: A person who favors the abolition of any institution, especially negro slavery.
absurdity: 1. The quality of being absurd or inconsistent with obvious truth, reason, or sound judgment. "The absurdity of the actual idea of an infinite number." Locke. 2. That which is absurd; an absurd action; a logical contradiction. His travels were full of absurdities. Johnson.
absinthium: The common wormwood (Artemisia absinthium), an intensely bitter plant, used as a tonic and for making the oil of wormwood.
abactor: One who steals and drives away cattle or beasts by herds or droves. (old)
abroad: 1. At large; widely; broadly; over a wide space; as, a tree spreads its branches abroad. The fox roams far abroad. Prior. 2. Without a certain confine; outside the house; away from one's abode; as, to walk abroad. I went to St. James', where another was preaching in the court abroad. Evelyn. 3. Beyond the bounds of a country; in foreign countries;
ablation: 1. A carrying or taking away; removal. Jer. Taylor. 2. (Med.) Extirpation. Dunglison. 3. (Geol.) Wearing away; superficial waste. Tyndall.
abettor: One who abets; an instigator of an offense or an offender. Note: The form abettor is the legal term and also in general use. Syn. -- Abettor, Accessory, Accomplice. These words denote different degrees of complicity in some deed or crime. An abettor is one who incites or encourages to the act, without sharing in its performance. An accessory supposes a principal offender.
abaculus: A small tile of glass, marble, or other substance, of various colors, used in making ornamental patterns in mosaic pavements. Fairholt.
ablet: A small fresh-water fish (Leuciscus alburnus); the bleak.
absoluteness: The quality of being absolute; independence of everything extraneous; unlimitedness; absolute power; independent reality; positiveness.
abandon: 1. To cast or drive out; to banish; to expel; to reject. (old) That he might . . . abandon them from him. Udall. Being all this time abandoned from your bed. Shak. 2. To give up absolutely; | Abandonment; relinquishment. (old)
absume: To consume gradually; to waste away. (old) Boyle.
abhal: The berries of a species of cypress in the East Indies.
abalienate: 1. (Civil Law) To transfer the title of from one to another; to alienate. 2. To estrange; to withdraw. (old) 3. To cause alienation of (mind). Sandys.
absinthiated: Impregnated with wormwood; as, absinthiated wine.
about: 1. Around; all round; on every side of. "Look about you." Shak. "Bind them about thy neck." Prov. iii. 3. 2. In the immediate neighborhood of; in contiguity or proximity to; near, as to place; | 1. On all sides; around. 'Tis time to look about. Shak. 2. In circuit; circularly; by a circuitous way; around the outside; as, a mile about, and a third of a mile across. 3. Here and there; around;
abutment: 1. State of abutting. 2. That on or against which a body abuts or presses; as (a) (Arch.) The solid part of a pier or wall, etc., which receives the thrust or lateral pressure of an arch, vault, or strut. Gwilt. (b) (mech.) A fixed point or surface from which resistance or reaction is obtained, as the cylinder head of a steam engine, the fulcrum of a lever, etc.
ablative: 1. Taking away or removing. (old) Where the heart is forestalled with misopinion, ablative directions are found needful to unteach error, ere we can learn truth. Bp. Hall. 2. | The ablative case. ablative absolute, a construction in Latin, in which a noun in the ablative case has a participle (either expressed or implied), agreeing with it in gender, number, and case, both…
absumption: Act of wasting away; a consuming; extinction. (old) Sir T. Browne.
abbreviation: 1. The act of shortening, or reducing. 2. The result of abbreviating; an abridgment. Tylor. 3. The form to which a word or phrase is reduced by contraction and omission; a letter or letters, standing for a word or phrase of which they are a part; as, Gen. for Genesis; U.S.A. for United States of America. 4.
absolutory: Serving to absolve; absolving. "An absolutory sentence." Ayliffe.
abusively: In an abusive manner; rudely; with abusive language.
aborigines: 1. The earliest known inhabitants of a country; native races. 2. The original fauna and flora of a geographical area
abutter: One who, or that which, abuts. Specifically, the owner of a contiguous estate; as, the abutters on a street or a river.
abroach: To set abroach; to let out, as liquor; to broach; to tap. (old) Chaucer. | 1. Broached; in a condition for letting out or yielding liquor, as a cask which is tapped. Hogsheads of ale were set abroach. Sir W. Scott. 2. Hence: In a state to be diffused or propagated; afoot;
abature: Grass and sprigs beaten or trampled down by a stag passing through them. Crabb.
abjudicate: To reject by judicial sentence; also, to abjudge. (old) Ash.
abduction: 1. The act of abducing or abducting; a drawing apart; a carrying away. Roget. 2. (Physiol.) The movement which separates a limb or other part from the axis, or middle line, of the body. 3. (Law) The wrongful, and usually the forcible, carrying off of a human being; as, the abduction of a child, the abduction of an heiress. 4.
abominable: 1. Worthy of, or causing, abhorrence, as a thing of evil omen; odious in the utmost degree; very hateful; detestable; loathsome; execrable. 2. Excessive; large; -- used as an intensive. (old) Note: Juliana Berners . . . informs us that in her time [15th c.], "abomynable syght of monkes" was elegant English for "a large company of friars." G. P. Marsh.
abject: 1. Cast down; low-lying. (old) From the safe shore their floating carcasses And broken chariot wheels; so thick bestrown Abject and lost lay these, covering the flood. Milton. 2. | To cast off or down; hence, to abase; to degrade; to lower; to debase. (old) Donne.
abuseful: Full of abuse; abusive. "Abuseful names." Bp. Barlow.
abruption: A sudden breaking off; a violent separation of bodies. Woodward.
abate: 1. To beat down; to overthrow. (old) The King of Scots . . . sore abated the walls. Edw. Hall. 2. To bring down or reduce from a higher to a lower state, number, or degree; to lessen; to diminish; | 1. To decrease, or become less in strength or violence; as, pain abates, a storm abates. The fury of Glengarry . . . rapidly abated. Macaulay. 2. To be defeated, or come to naught; to fall through;
abstinence: 1. The act or practice of abstaining; voluntary forbearance of any action, especially the refraining from an indulgence of appetite, or from customary gratifications of animal or sensual propensities. Specifically, the practice of abstaining from intoxicating beverages, -- called also total abstinence.
abracadabra: A mystical word or collocation of letters written as in the figure. Worn on an amulet it was supposed to ward off fever. At present the word is used chiefly in jest to denote something without meaning; jargon.
abortive: 1. Produced by abortion; born prematurely; as, an abortive child. 2. Made from the skin of a still-born animal; as, abortive vellum. (old) 3. Rendering fruitless or ineffectual. | 1. That which is born or brought forth prematurely; an abortion. (old) Shak. 2. A fruitless effort or issue. (old) 3. A medicine to which is attributed the property of causing abortion. Dunglison.
absorptive: Having power, capacity, or tendency to absorb or imbibe. E. Darwin.
abysmally: To a fathomless depth; profoundly. "Abysmally ignorant." G. Eliot.
abolish: 1. To do away with wholly; to annul; to make void; -- said of laws, customs, institutions, governments, etc.; as, to abolish slavery, to abolish folly. 2. To put an end to, or destroy, as a physical objects; to wipe out. (old) And with thy blood abolish so reproachful blot. Spenser. His quick instinctive hand Caught at the hilt, as to abolish him. Tennyson. Syn.
abusion: Evil or corrupt usage; abuse; wrong; reproach; deception; cheat. Chaucer.
absently: In an absent or abstracted manner.
absorbent: Absorbing; swallowing; absorptive. Absorbent ground (Paint.), a ground prepared for a picture, chiefly with distemper, or water colors, by which the oil is absorbed, and a brilliancy is imparted to… | 1. Anything which absorbs. The ocean, itself a bad absorbent of heat. Darwin. 2. (Med.) Any substance which absorbs and neutralizes acid fluid in the stomach and bowels, as magnesia, chalk, etc.;
absinthe: 1. The plant absinthium or common wormwood. 2. A strong spirituous liqueur made from wormwood and brandy or alcohol.
absonant: Discordant; contrary; -- opposed to consonant. "Absonant to nature." Quarles.
absolutism: 1. The state of being absolute; the system or doctrine of the absolute; the principles or practice of absolute or arbitrary government; despotism. The element of absolutism and prelacy was controlling. Palfrey. 2. (Theol.) Doctrine of absolute decrees. Ash.
abbess: A female superior or governess of a nunnery, or convent of nuns, having the same authority over the nuns which the abbots have over the monks. See Abbey.
abscissa: One of the elements of reference by which a point, as of a curve, is referred to a system of fixed rectilineal coördinate axes. Note: When referred to two intersecting axes, one of them called the axis of abscissas, or of X, and the other the axis of ordinates, or of Y, the abscissa of the point is the distance cut off from the axis of X by a line drawn through it and parallel…
absist: To stand apart from; top leave off; to desist. (old) Raleigh.
aboveboard: Above the board or table. Hence: in open sight; without trick, concealment, or deception. "Fair and aboveboard." Burke. Note: This expression is said by Johnson to have been borrowed from gamesters, who, when they change their cards, put their hands under the table.
absentminded: Absent in mind; abstracted; preoccupied. -- Ab`sent-mind"ed*ness, n. -- Ab`sent-mind"ed*ly, adv.
absorb: 1. To swallow up; to engulf; to overwhelm; to cause to disappear as if by swallowing up; to use up; to include. "Dark oblivion soon absorbs them all." Cowper. The large cities absorb the wealth and fashion. W. Irving. 2. To suck up; to drink in; to imbibe; as a sponge or as the lacteals of the body. Bacon. 3. To engross or engage wholly; to occupy fully;
abrogation: The act of abrogating; repeal by authority. Hume.
abassis: A silver coin of Persia, worth about twenty cents.
abdicant: Abdicating; renouncing; -- followed by of. Monks abdicant of their orders. Whitlock.
abaxile: Away from the axis or central line; eccentric. Balfour.
abomasum: The fourth or digestive stomach of a ruminant, which leads from the third stomach omasum. See Ruminantia.
abductor: 1. One who abducts. 2. (Anat.) A muscle which serves to draw a part out, or form the median line of the body; as, the abductor oculi, which draws the eye outward.
abridge: 1. To make shorter; to shorten in duration; to lessen; to diminish; to curtail; as, to abridge labor; to abridge power or rights. "The bridegroom . . . abridged his visit." Smollett. She retired herself to Sebaste, and abridged her train from state to necessity. Fuller. 2. To shorten or contract by using fewer words, yet retaining the sense; to epitomize; to condense;
abscission: 1. The act or process of cutting off. "Not to be cured without the abscission of a member." Jer. Taylor. 2. The state of being cut off. Sir T. Browne. 3. (Rhet.) A figure of speech employed when a speaker having begun to say a thing stops abruptly: thus, "He is a man of so much honor and candor, and of such generosity -- but I need say no more."
absolutist: 1. One who is in favor of an absolute or autocratic government. 2. (Metaph.) One who believes that it is possible to realize a cognition or concept of the absolute. Sir. W. Hamilton. | Of or pertaining to absolutism; arbitrary; despotic; as, absolutist principles.
abhor: 1. To shrink back with shuddering from; to regard with horror or detestation; to feel excessive repugnance toward; to detest to extremity; to loathe. Abhor that which is evil; | To shrink back with horror, disgust, or dislike; to be contrary or averse; -- with from. (old) "To abhor from those vices." Udall. Which is utterly abhorring from the end of all law. Milton.
absenteeism: The state or practice of an absentee; esp. the practice of absenting one's self from the country or district where one's estate is situated.
abhorring: 1. Detestation. Milton. 2. Object of abhorrence. Isa. lxvi. 24.
abut: To project; to terminate or border; to be contiguous; to meet; -- with on, upon, or against; as, his land abuts on the road.
abluent: Washing away; carrying off impurities; detergent. -- n. (Med.) A detergent.
abuna: The Patriarch, or head of the Abyssinian Church.
abstain: To hold one's self aloof; to forbear or refrain voluntarily, and especially from an indulgence of the passions or appetites; -- with from. Not a few abstained from voting. Macaulay. | To hinder; to withhold. Whether he abstain men from marrying. Milton.
abominate: To turn from as ill-omened; to hate in the highest degree, as if with religious dread; loathe; as, to abominate all impiety. Syn. -- To hate; abhor; loathe; detest. See Hate.
absorbedly: In a manner as if wholly engrossed or engaged.
abarticulation: Articulation, usually that kind of articulation which admits of free motion in the joint; diarthrosis. Coxe.
absorber: One who, or that which, absorbs.
abstrusity: Abstruseness; that which is abstruse. Sir T. Browne.
abnegate: To deny and reject; to abjure. Sir E. Sandys. Farrar.
absorbable: Capable of being absorbed or swallowed up. Kerr.
absolve: 1. To set free, or release, as from some obligation, debt, or responsibility, or from the consequences of guilt or such ties as it would be sin or guilt to violate; to pronounce free; as, to absolve a subject from his allegiance; to absolve an offender, which amounts to an acquittal and remission of his punishment. Halifax was absolved by a majority of fourteen. Macaulay. 2.
abscondence: Fugitive concealment; secret retirement; hiding. Phillips.
absolute: 1. Loosed from any limitation or condition; uncontrolled; unrestricted; unconditional; as, absolute authority, monarchy, sovereignty, an absolute promise or command; absolute power; | In a plane, the two imaginary circular points at infinity; in space of three dimensions, the imaginary circle at infinity.
abstersion: Act of wiping clean; a cleansing; a purging. The task of ablution and abstersion being performed. Sir W. Scott.
abolition: The act of abolishing, or the state of being abolished; an annulling; abrogation; utter destruction; as, the abolition of slavery or the slave trade; the abolition of laws, decrees, ordinances, customs, taxes, debts, etc. Note: The application of this word to persons is now unusual or obsolete
abeyance: 1. (Law) Expectancy; condition of being undetermined. Note: When there is no person in existence in whom an inheritance (or a dignity) can vest, it is said to be in abeyance, that is, in expectation; the law considering it as always potentially existing, and ready to vest whenever a proper owner appears. Blackstone. 2. Suspension; temporary suppression.
abye: 1. To pay for; to suffer for; to atone for; to make amends for; to give satisfaction. (old) Lest to thy peril thou aby it dear. Shak. 2. To endure; to abide. (old) But nought that wanteth rest can long aby. Spenser.
abdominothoracic: Relating to the abdomen and the thorax, or chest.
abruptness: 1. The state of being abrupt or broken; craggedness; ruggedness; steepness. 2. Suddenness; unceremonious haste or vehemence; as, abruptness of style or manner.
abrade: To rub or wear off; to waste or wear away by friction; as, to abrade rocks. Lyell.
abstrusion: The act of thrusting away. Ogilvie.
ablaqueation: The act or process of laying bare the roots of trees to expose them to the air and water. (old) Evelyn.
abbreviature: 1. An abbreviation; an abbreviated state or form. (old) 2. An abridgment; a compendium or abstract. This is an excellent abbreviature of the whole duty of a Christian. Jer. Taylor.
aboral: Situated opposite to, or away from, the mouth.
abbe: The French word answering to the English abbot, the head of an abbey; but commonly a title of respect given in France to every one vested with the ecclesiastical habit or dress. Note: * After the 16th century, the name was given, in social parlance, to candidates for some priory or abbey in the gift of the crown.
abear: 1. To bear; to behave. (old) So did the faery knight himself abear. Spenser. 2. To put up with; to endure. [Prov.] Dickens.
abyssinian: Of or pertaining to Abyssinia. Abyssinian gold, an alloy of 90.74 parts of copper and 8.33 parts of zink. Ure. | 1. A native of Abyssinia. 2. A member of the Abyssinian Church.
abstract: 1. Withdraw; separate. (old) The more abstract . . . we are from the body. Norris. 2. Considered apart from any application to a particular object; separated from matter; exiting in the mind only; | 1. To withdraw; to separate; to take away. He was incapable of forming any opinion or resolution abstracted from his own prejudices. Sir W. Scott. 2. To draw off in respect to interest or attention;
absquatulate: To take one's self off; to decamp. [A jocular word. U. S.]
absinthian: Of the nature of wormwood. "Absinthian bitterness." T. Randolph.
abraum: A red ocher used to darken mahogany and for making chloride of potassium.
abjuration: 1. The act of abjuring or forswearing; a renunciation upon oath; as, abjuration of the realm, a sworn banishment, an oath taken to leave the country and never to return. 2. A solemn recantation or renunciation; as, an abjuration of heresy.
abiogenetic: Of or pertaining to abiogenesis. Ab`i*o*ge*net"ic*al*ly, adv.
abietinic: Of or pertaining to abietin; as, abietinic acid.
aberdevine: The European siskin (Carduelis spinus), a small green and yellow finch, related to the goldfinch.
abditive: Having the quality of hiding. Bailey.
abjectedness: A very abject or low condition; abjectness. Boyle.
abnormity: Departure from the ordinary type; irregularity; monstrosity. "An abnormity . . . like a calf born with two heads." Mrs. Whitney.
abaddon: 1. The destroyer, or angel of the bottomless pit; -- the same as Apollyon and Asmodeus. 2. Hell; the bottomless pit. (poetic) In all her gates, Abaddon rues Thy bold attempt. Milton.
abortively: In an abortive or untimely manner; immaturely; fruitlessly.
abloom: In or into bloom; in a blooming state. Masson.
abietin: A resinous obtained from Strasburg turpentine or Canada balsam. It is without taste or smell, is insoluble in water, but soluble in alcohol (especially at the boiling point), in strong acetic acid, and in ether. Watts.
abolitionize: To imbue with the principles of abolitionism. Bartlett.
abbreviator: 1. One who abbreviates or shortens. 2. One of a college of seventy-two officers of the papal court whose duty is to make a short minute of a decision on a petition, or reply of the pope to a letter, and afterwards expand the minute into official form.
abort: 1. To miscarry; to bring forth young prematurely. 2. (Biol.) To become checked in normal development, so as either to remain rudimentary or shrink away wholly; to become sterile. | 1. An untimely birth. (old) Sir H. Wotton. 2. An aborted offspring. (old) Holland.
abysmal: Pertaining to, or resembling, an abyss; bottomless; unending; profound. Geology gives one the same abysmal extent of time that astronomy does of space. Carlyle.
abundantly: In a sufficient degree; fully; amply; plentifully; in large measure.
ablatitious: Diminishing; as, an ablatitious force. Sir J. Herschel.
abed: 1. In bed, or on the bed. Not to be abed after midnight. Shak. 2. To childbed (in the phrase "brought abed," that is, delivered of a child). Shak.
abba: Father; religious superior; -- in the Syriac, Coptic, and Ethiopic churches, a title given to the bishops, and by the bishops to the patriarch.
abeyant: Being in a state of abeyance.
abactinal: Pertaining to the surface or end opposite to the mouth in a radiate animal; -- opposed to actinal. "The aboral or abactinal area." L. Agassiz.
abridgment: 1. The act abridging, or the state of being abridged; diminution; lessening; reduction or deprivation; as, an abridgment of pleasures or of expenses. 2. An epitome or compend, as of a book; a shortened or abridged form; an abbreviation. Ancient coins as abridgments of history. Addison. 3. That which abridges or cuts short;
abstruseness: The quality of being abstruse; difficulty of apprehension. Boyle.
abysm: An abyss; a gulf. "The abysm of hell." Shak.
abortifacient: Producing miscarriage. -- n. A drug or an agent that causes premature delivery.
aby: 1. To pay for; to suffer for; to atone for; to make amends for; to give satisfaction. (old) Lest to thy peril thou aby it dear. Shak. 2. To endure; to abide. (old) But nought that wanteth rest can long aby. Spenser.
abdominal: 1. Of or pertaining to the abdomen; ventral; as, the abdominal regions, muscles, cavity. 2. (Zoöl.) Having abdominal fins; belonging to the Abdominales; as, abdominal fishes. | A fish of the group Abdominales.
absinthic: Relating to the common wormwood or to an acid obtained from it.
aband: 1. To abandon. (old) Enforced the kingdom to aband. Spenser. 2. To banish; to expel. (old) Mir. for Mag.
abovecited: Cited before, in the preceding part of a book or writing.
abduct: 1. To take away surreptitiously by force; to carry away (a human being) wrongfully and usually by violence; to kidnap. 2. To draw away, as a limb or other part, from its ordinary position.
aborted: 1. Brought forth prematurely. 2. (Biol.) Rendered abortive or sterile; undeveloped; checked in normal development at a very early stage; as, spines are aborted branches. The eyes of the cirripeds are more or less aborted in their mature state. Owen.
abra: A narrow pass or defile; a break in a mesa; the mouth of a cañon. [Southwestern U. S.]
abietite: A substance resembling mannite, found in the needles of the common silver fir of Europe (Abies pectinata). Eng. Cyc.
ablution: 1. The act of washing or cleansing; specifically, the washing of the body, or some part of it, as a religious rite. 2. The water used in cleansing. "Cast the ablutions in the main." Pope. 3. (R. C.
abaiser: Ivory black or animal charcoal. Weale.
abovedeck: On deck; and hence, like aboveboard, without artifice. Smart.
absorbability: The state or quality of being absorbable. Graham (Chemistry).
abligate: To tie up so as to hinder from. (old)
ablegate: A representative of the pope charged with important commissions in foreign countries, one of his duties being to bring to a newly named cardinal his insignia of office.
abet: 1. To instigate or encourage by aid or countenance; -- used in a bad sense of persons and acts; as, to abet an ill-doer; to abet one in his wicked courses; to abet vice; to abet an insurrection. | Act of abetting; aid. (old) Chaucer.
abreast: 1. Side by side, with breasts in a line; as, "Two men could hardly walk abreast." Macaulay. 2. (Naut.) Side by side; also, opposite; over against; on a line with the vessel's beam; -- with of. 3. Up to a certain level or line; equally advanced; as, to keep abreast of [or with] the present state of science. 4. At the same time; simultaneously.
abstractively: In a abstract manner; separately; in or by itself. Feltham.
absentness: The quality of being absent-minded. H. Miller.
absentment: The state of being absent; withdrawal. Barrow.
abstainer: One who abstains; esp., one who abstains from the use of intoxicating liquors.
aberrate: To go astray; to diverge. Their own defective and aberrating vision. De Quincey.
aberrance: State of being aberrant; a wandering from the right way; deviation from truth, rectitude, etc. Aberrancy of curvature (Geom.), the deviation of a curve from a circular form.
abnormality: 1. The state or quality of being abnormal; variation; irregularity. Darwin. 2. Something abnormal.
absurd: Contrary to reason or propriety; obviously and fiatly opposed to manifest truth; inconsistent with the plain dictates of common sense; logically contradictory; nonsensical; ridiculous; as, an absurd person, an absurd opinion; an absurd dream. This proffer is absurd and reasonless. Shak. 'This phrase absurd to call a villain great. Pope. p. 9 Syn. -- Foolish; irrational;
abb: Among weaves, yarn for the warp. Hence, abb wool is wool for the abb.
abomination: 1. The feeling of extreme disgust and hatred; abhorrence; detestation; loathing; as, he holds tobacco in abomination. 2. That which is abominable; anything hateful, wicked, or shamefully vile; an object or state that excites disgust and hatred; a hateful or shameful vice; pollution. Antony, most large in his abominations. Shak. 3. A cause of pollution or wickedness. Syn.
abradant: A material used for grinding, as emery, sand, powdered glass, etc.
abbot: 1. The superior or head of an abbey. 2. One of a class of bishops whose sees were formerly abbeys. Encyc. Brit. Abbot of the people. a title formerly given to one of the chief magistrates in Genoa. -- Abbot of Misrule (or Lord of Misrule), in mediæval times, the master of revels, as at Christmas; in Scotland called the Abbot of Unreason. Encyc. Brit.
abay: Barking; baying of dogs upon their prey. See Bay. (old)
absquehoc: . Etym: [L., without this.] (Law) The technical words of denial used in traversing what has been alleged, and is repeated.
aboon: and adv. Above. [Scot. & Prov. Eng.] Aboon the pass of Bally-Brough. Sir W. Scott. The ceiling fair that rose aboon. J. R. Drake.
abib: The first month of the Jewish ecclesiastical year, corresponding nearly to our April. After the Babylonish captivity this month was called Nisan. Kitto.
abdal: A religious devotee or dervish in Persia.
absinthism: The condition of being poisoned by the excessive use of absinth.
abode: 1. Act of waiting; delay. (old) Shak. And with her fled away without abode. Spenser. 2. Stay or continuance in a place; sojourn. He waxeth at your abode here. Fielding. 3. | An omen. (old) High-thundering Juno's husband stirs my spirit with true abodes. Chapman.
abashment: The state of being abashed; confusion from shame.
abiological: Pertaining to the study of inanimate things.
abyssal: Belonging to, or resembling, an abyss; unfathomable. Abyssal zone (Phys. Geog.), one of the belts or zones into which Sir E. Forbes divides the bottom of the sea in describing its plants, animals, etc. It is the one furthest from the shore, embracing all beyond one hundred fathoms deep. Hence, abyssal animals, plants, etc.
abundant: Fully sufficient; plentiful; in copious supply; -- followed by in, rarely by with. "Abundant in goodness and truth." Exod. xxxiv. 6. Abundant number (Math.), a number, the sum of whose aliquot parts exceeds the number itself. Thus, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, the aliquot parts of 12, make the number 16.
absterse: To absterge; to cleanse; to purge away. (old) Sir T. Browne.
abjudge: To take away by judicial decision.
abomasus: The fourth or digestive stomach of a ruminant, which leads from the third stomach omasum. See Ruminantia.
